title: Unhealthy instances
prompt: You are given heartbeat records from production instances. Return the unique instance ids that are unhealthy, in the order they first appear. An instance is unhealthy if any of its records has healthy=False, cpu at or above the threshold, or last_heartbeat_seconds greater than 120. Missing optional fields are not enough to mark it unhealthy. Ignore unknown keys.
constraints: Return unique instance ids in the order they first appear.
An instance is unhealthy if any record has healthy=False, CPU at or above the threshold, or last_heartbeat_seconds greater than 120.
Missing optional fields are not enough to mark it unhealthy.
Ignore unknown keys.
Do not modify the input. All records have valid identifiers and numeric metrics when present.
hints: An instance is unhealthy when any one of its records fails a policy. Policies are independent: a false healthy flag, CPU at or above the threshold, or a heartbeat older than 120 seconds.
Walk the list once. Remember every instance id in first-seen order, and remember which ids have already failed a policy. Build a new list; do not edit the input records.

Keep an ordered map (or list plus set) of first-seen ids, and a set of unhealthy ids. After the scan, emit ordered ids that also sit in the unhealthy set. For missing fields, use the defaults in the criteria instead of inventing failure.
explanation: Evaluate each policy on each record without short-circuiting the others out of existence in your head. Preserve first-seen order from the full input, including ids whose first observation was healthy. Build a fresh list so the caller's records stay untouched.

title: A deploy that should stop
prompt: Your platform team runs an offline check before a batch rollout. Work on the Python checker using normalized deployment records. Report unsafe defaults without changing the input. This exercise runs against fixtures, not a live cluster.
constraints: Each record has a unique name. Other fields may be missing; numeric fields contain numbers when present.
Report no_replicas when replicas is missing or at most zero.
Report no_readiness_probe unless readiness_probe is True.
Report no_memory_limit when memory_limit_mib is missing or at most zero.
Return {name, issues} for unsafe deployments only. Keep input order and issue order: replicas, readiness, memory.
Do not mutate the input or contact a cluster.
Do not modify the input. All records have valid identifiers and numeric metrics when present.
hints: You are auditing defaults, not talking to a cluster. Each rule names a concrete issue code. A deployment with no issues must not appear in the result.
For each record, collect issues in a fixed order: replicas, then readiness, then memory. Append {name, issues} only when that list is non-empty, preserving the input order of deployments.
Sketch three independent ifs that append issue codes, then append the result row only if issues is non-empty. Do not mutate the input dicts.
explanation: Each rule is a local predicate on one record. Keep issue codes in the documented order so downstream tooling can match them. Skip healthy deployments entirely instead of returning empty issue lists.
complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output/auxiliary space.
followUp: How would you verify a change before a fleet-wide rollout?
situation: This offline checker runs before a batch rollout. A miss lets an unsafe Deployment ship; a false positive blocks a safe one.
guarantee: Return only deployments that fail at least one rule, each as {name, issues}, keeping input order and the fixed issue order: replicas, readiness, memory.

readiness_probe must be exactly True; anything else → no_readiness_probe.

title: HTTP status counts
prompt: Summarize normalized access-log records for an incident report. Count records in each HTTP status class.
constraints: Each record has integer status from 100 to 599. Return only observed classes as string keys such as "2xx".
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: HTTP status classes are hundreds: 200–299 share class 2, 500–599 share class 5.
One pass is enough. Use a dictionary from class to count, then return the structure the examples show.
For each record, key = status // 100; counts[key] = counts.get(key, 0) + 1. Skip building entries for classes you never saw.
explanation: Aggregate by status // 100. Empty input produces an empty mapping; missing traffic is not a healthy percentage.
complexity: O(n) time; at most five counters.
followUp: What additional information would distinguish no traffic from missing telemetry?
situation: Status codes land in dashboards as class counts. A wrong bucket makes a 5xx spike look like a 4xx or hides it.
guarantee: Map each status into its hundred-class and count how many records fall in each class that appears.
edges: Integer division by 100 is the class key.
Classes with zero count must not appear.
Do not mutate the input list.
failureGuide: Confirm the class key is status // 100 and that unused classes are omitted.

constraints: Records have service (string) and status (integer). Count statuses 500–599 only. Return service names by count descending, then name ascending for ties.

Count per service, then sort with a key that prefers higher counts and breaks ties by name.
After counting, sort with key=(-count, name) or the language equivalent, and return the ranked shape the examples use.
explanation: Count customer-visible server errors and sort the aggregated keys. This ranks volume, not error ratio.
complexity: O(n + s log s) time, O(s) space.
followUp: Why might a low-traffic service with 100% failures rank below a healthier busy service?
situation: On-call sorts services by error volume. A wrong rank sends people into the quiet service first.
guarantee: Count only records that count as errors, then rank services by descending count and ascending name on ties.
edges: Filter before you count.
Tie-break is lexicographic service name.
Services with zero errors do not appear.
failureGuide: Check the filter, then the sort key (negative count, then name).

title: A latency percentile
prompt: Calculate a tail-latency statistic from a bounded batch of raw millisecond measurements.
constraints: Values are nonnegative numbers; 0 < p <= 100. Return sorted[ceil(p*n/100)-1]. Return None for no samples.

Copy and sort the values ascending. Translate the percentile into a one-based rank, then into a zero-based index.
If n == 0: return None. Else index = ceil(p*n/100) - 1 on the sorted copy, then return sorted[index].

followUp: Why does a histogram-derived p95 differ from an exact percentile of raw samples?

guarantee: On a copy of the samples, return the nearest-rank value at ceil(p*n/100), or None when there are no samples.
edges: Empty input returns None.
Never sort the caller's list in place.
Nearest rank uses ceiling, then a zero-based index.
failureGuide: Sort a copy, compute ceil(p*n/100)-1, and confirm empty input returns None.

title: Failures in a rolling window
prompt: Implement the event selection behind a rolling error counter.
constraints: Events contain timestamp (integer seconds) and status. Count 500–599 when now-window < timestamp <= now. Events may be unsorted. window is positive.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: A window is a closed interval on the timeline ending at now, not every event you have ever seen.
Compute the oldest acceptable timestamp once, then count events that sit between that bound and now.
start = now - window; count events with start <= t <= now. Do not count t > now.
explanation: A half-open boundary avoids counting an event twice at adjoining interval edges. Future telemetry must not enter the current window.
complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
followUp: How would you update this efficiently for a timestamp-sorted continuous stream?
solution:
def window_errors(events, now, window):
    return sum(1 for event in events if now - window < event["timestamp"] <= now and 500 <= event["status"] <= 599)
situation: A rolling error window drives burn alerts. Including future or stale events changes whether you page.
guarantee: Count only events whose timestamps sit inside the inclusive window ending at now.
edges: Exclude timestamps older than the window start.
Exclude timestamps after now.
Write both boundaries before looping.
failureGuide: Check both window edges: too old and still in the future.

title: Error budget left
prompt: Report how many additional failed requests fit into a request-based error budget.
constraints: total and failures are nonnegative integers; failures <= total. slo_bps is 0–10000 basis points. Allowed failures = floor(total*(10000-slo_bps)/10000). Return allowed minus failures, including negative values.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Budget remaining is allowed budget minus observed failures, expressed with the SLO in basis points.
Prefer integer math so floating point cannot nudge a boundary. A negative result means the budget is already spent.
allowed = total * slo_bps // 10000; return allowed - failures without max(0, …).
explanation: Basis points make the contract exact. Integer floor prevents promising a fractional failed request.
complexity: O(1) time and space.
followUp: Why does a request-based budget differ from a time-based availability budget?
solution:
def remaining_budget(total, failures, slo_bps):
    return total * (10000 - slo_bps) // 10000 - failures
situation: Error budget is how much failure SLO still allows. Clamping or floating drift changes whether a release may ship.
guarantee: Compute remaining budget in integers from total, failures, and slo_bps. Negative remainders are valid evidence.
edges: Keep arithmetic in integers.
Do not clamp a negative budget to zero.
Basis points mean / 10000, not / 100.
failureGuide: Re-check integer arithmetic and whether a negative remainder was clamped away.

Put received timestamps in a set. Walk the theoretical schedule from start through end by interval.
expected = start, start+interval, … while <= end; emit those missing from the received set, in schedule order.

followUp: How would clock skew change the definition of a missed heartbeat?

guarantee: Return the expected heartbeat timestamps in [start, end] that never appear in the received set.
edges: Generate the schedule from start, end, and interval; do not infer it only from observations.
Membership checks belong on a set of received timestamps.
Do not mutate the input list.

title: Capped retry delays
prompt: Prepare a deterministic exponential-backoff schedule. This function computes delays; it does not sleep or send requests.
constraints: attempts, base_ms and cap_ms are nonnegative integers. Attempt zero waits min(base_ms, cap_ms); each later delay doubles until capped. Return one delay per retry.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Each entry is how long to wait before that retry, not including the original try.
Start from base_ms, double after each entry, and replace any value above cap_ms with the cap before recording it.
delays = []; delay = base_ms; for _ in range(attempts): delay = min(delay, cap_ms); delays.append(delay); delay *= 2.
explanation: Capping before the next iteration avoids ever-growing integers. Production clients also need jitter, a retry budget and an overall deadline.
complexity: O(attempts) time and output space.
followUp: When would retrying a failed request be unsafe even with backoff?
solution:
def retry_delays(attempts, base_ms, cap_ms):
    delays = []
    delay = min(base_ms, cap_ms)
    for _ in range(attempts):
        delays.append(delay)
        delay = min(delay * 2, cap_ms)
    return delays
situation: Retry delays shape client storms. An uncapped or off-by-one sequence either hammers a dependency or gives up too soon.
guarantee: Return the delay before each retry attempt, doubling from base_ms and never exceeding cap_ms. Zero attempts means an empty list.
edges: Carry the capped delay forward so the next doubling starts from the cap.
attempts == 0 yields [].
The list length equals attempts.
failureGuide: Check length, doubling, and that the cap sticks on later attempts.

title: A token bucket
prompt: Decide whether each timestamped request is admitted by a per-process token bucket.
constraints: Timestamps are nonnegative seconds in nondecreasing order. capacity is a positive integer; refill_per_second is nonnegative. Start full at time 0. Refill to capacity before each request; admitting consumes one token. Return booleans.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: A token bucket allows a short burst up to capacity while limiting the long-run rate.
Keep current tokens and the last timestamp you considered. On each request, refill from elapsed time, then decide.
On each t: tokens = min(capacity, tokens + (t - last) * refill); last = t; if tokens >= 1: tokens -= 1; admit else reject.
explanation: A bucket permits a burst up to capacity while limiting long-run rate. Refill is based on elapsed time, even after a rejected request.
complexity: O(n) time; O(1) state excluding output.
followUp: How would you coordinate this policy across multiple API replicas?
solution:
def admit_requests(timestamps, capacity, refill_per_second):
    tokens, previous = capacity, 0
    result = []
    for timestamp in timestamps:
        tokens = min(capacity, tokens + (timestamp - previous) * refill_per_second)
        allowed = tokens >= 1
        result.append(allowed)
        if allowed:
            tokens -= 1
        previous = timestamp
    return result
situation: Admission control protects a process from burst overload. Admitting a rejected request, or refilling on a reject, breaks the limit.
guarantee: Start full at time 0. Before each request, refill by elapsed time up to capacity; admitting spends one token; rejects spend none.
edges: Rejected requests do not consume tokens.
Simultaneous requests do not get a magical extra refill between them.
Timestamps are nondecreasing.
failureGuide: Track tokens and last time. Refill before the decision; only successful admits decrement.

title: When the circuit opens
prompt: Locate the first point at which consecutive failures would open a simplified circuit breaker.
constraints: outcomes contains booleans: True is success, False is failure. threshold is a positive integer. Return the zero-based index of the first threshold-length failure streak, or None. Success resets the streak.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Opening is about a run of failures in a row, not how many failures exist in the whole list.
Scan left to right with a counter. Increment on failure, reset on success, and stop when the counter hits threshold.
streak = 0; for i, outcome in enumerate(...): streak = streak+1 if failure else 0; if streak == threshold: return i.
explanation: A consecutive-failure policy is a simplified breaker trigger. A real breaker also needs an open duration and half-open probes.
complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space.
followUp: When might a rolling error ratio be a better trigger than consecutive failures?
situation: Circuit breakers open on consecutive failures, not lifetime totals. Counting the wrong thing trips early or never.
guarantee: Return the index where the consecutive failure streak first reaches threshold, or the refusal the examples use when it never does.
edges: A success resets the streak to zero.
Total failure count is not the streak.
Threshold is consecutive outcomes.
failureGuide: Reset on success. Compare the streak to threshold at each failure.

title: Overlapping maintenance windows
prompt: Combine overlapping or touching maintenance windows into a minimal list for a status page.
constraints: Each window is [start, end] with start <= end. Input may be unsorted. Touching windows merge. Return merged windows in ascending start order.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Merging is a sweep over intervals ordered by start, not a pairwise check of every combination.
Sort a copy. Keep a current merged interval and either extend its end or push it and start a new one.
After sorting, for each [s,e]: if s <= current_end: current_end = max(current_end, e); else append current and start [s,e].
explanation: The invariant is that finished intervals cannot overlap any remaining interval. Copy interval values so extending a result does not mutate input.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.
followUp: Would touching windows still merge if they belonged to different services?
situation: Overlapping maintenance windows double-book change freezes. Merging them wrong leaves gaps or invents coverage.
guarantee: Merge overlapping or touching intervals into a minimal sorted list of disjoint windows.
edges: Sort a copy by start time.
Compare each interval to the end of the current merged interval.
Do not mutate the caller's list.
failureGuide: Sort by start, then extend or append based on overlap with the current end.

title: Service startup order
prompt: Plan startup for services whose dependencies must be ready first. Detect cycles rather than waiting forever.
constraints: Input maps every service name to a list of dependency names; every dependency is also a key. Lists have no duplicates. Choose the lexicographically smallest currently ready service at each step. Return None if there is a cycle.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: This is Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly start a service whose remaining dependencies are already up.
Track how many dependencies each service still needs, plus reverse edges to decrement dependents. Use a min-structure for the ready set.
While ready: pop the smallest name, append it, decrement dependents, and enqueue those that hit zero. If len(order) < len(services): return None.
explanation: Kahn’s algorithm repeatedly removes a ready vertex. Counting all emitted vertices detects cycles even when a different component can start.
complexity: O((V + E) log V) time, O(V + E) space.
followUp: How would you distinguish a dependency cycle from a service that is merely slow to become ready?
situation: Service boot order with a cycle hangs forever. A wrong topological order starts a dependent before its dependency.
guarantee: Emit a valid startup order choosing the lexicographically smallest ready service at each step, or None when a cycle remains.
edges: Every dependency name is also a key.
Tie-break is lexicographically smallest ready name.
If you emit fewer than all services, return None.
failureGuide: Check indegrees, the ready-set tie-break, and cycle detection via emit count.

title: Peak work in flight
prompt: Estimate the maximum simultaneously active requests from completed request intervals.
constraints: Each interval is [start, end) with start <= end. Zero-length intervals count as no work. An end at time t is processed before a start at t. Return the maximum active count.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Peak concurrency is the deepest overlap on a timeline, not the number of intervals.
Turn each interval into a start event and an end event, sort them, and sweep while tracking current depth.
Events = (+1 at start, -1 at end); sort by time, and for equal time put -1 before +1; track cur and max.
explanation: The half-open convention matters at ties. Ignoring zero-length work prevents negative counts from isolated equal-time events.
complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
followUp: Why is peak concurrency insufficient to determine a sustainable worker-pool size?
situation: Peak in-flight work sizes pools and autoscales. Counting ends after starts at the same timestamp understates the peak.
guarantee: Return the maximum number of intervals that overlap at any instant, treating an end before a start at the same time.
edges: Convert intervals into start and end events.
At equal timestamps, process ends before starts.
Do not mutate the input.
failureGuide: Sort ends before starts at equal times, then walk the sweep counting depth.

title: Configuration drift
prompt: Compare two flat configuration maps before reconciling a service.
constraints: Return sorted keys that are missing on either side or have unequal JSON scalar values. Missing is different from a present None. Values have consistent types when a key exists in both maps.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Drift includes keys present on only one side, not only unequal shared values.
Take the union of keys. For each key, classify missing-desired, missing-actual, or unequal.
for key in sorted(set(desired) | set(actual)): compare membership first, then values when both exist.
explanation: A default of None conflates absence with an explicit null. Membership captures the operational distinction.
complexity: O(k log k) time, O(k) space.
followUp: Which configuration fields should be ignored because a controller owns them?
solution:
def config_drift(desired, actual):
    return sorted(key for key in desired.keys() | actual.keys() if key not in desired or key not in actual or desired[key] != actual[key])
situation: Desired versus actual config drift is how silent misconfig ships. Missing keys are drift too.
guarantee: Report keys that differ or exist on only one side, using the structure the examples show.
edges: Inspect the union of keys.
Membership checks come before value compares.
Do not mutate either mapping.
failureGuide: Walk desired ∪ actual. Absent on one side is drift even when the other value looks fine.

title: Duplicate webhook deliveries
prompt: Keep the first delivery of each incident event so repeated webhook delivery does not duplicate notifications.
constraints: Each event has a string id and arbitrary JSON fields. Return complete first-seen records in input order. Later copies of an id are ignored even if their payload differs.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Idempotent intake keeps the first copy of an id and ignores the rest.
Maintain a set of ids you have already emitted, and append to the result only on first sight.
seen = set(); out = []; for event in events: if id not in seen: seen.add(id); out.append(event).
explanation: An idempotency key defines duplicate identity. This in-memory implementation is a batch exercise; production needs durable state and retention.
complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space.
followUp: What happens if a process crashes after sending a notification but before saving the idempotency key?
situation: Duplicate deliveries inflate metrics and fan-out. Sorting them rewrites history; dropping the first delivery loses the real event.
guarantee: Keep the first record for each event id and preserve first-delivery order.
edges: Track seen ids separately from the output list.
Do not sort by id or timestamp unless the contract says so.
Later duplicates are dropped entirely.
failureGuide: First delivery wins. Output order follows first appearance, not sorted ids.

title: Keys on shards
prompt: Build a deterministic modulo router for a batch of integer tenant IDs.
constraints: shard_count is positive; keys are nonnegative integers. Return a mapping with string shard indexes for nonempty shards only. Assign key % shard_count and preserve key order within each shard. Keep duplicates.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Routing here is deterministic placement, not load-aware balancing.
For each key, compute a non-negative index from the key and the shard count.
return [key % shard_count for key in keys] with the language's integer modulo rules matching the fixtures.
explanation: Modulo routing is simple and deterministic. Changing the shard count moves many keys; this is deliberately not consistent hashing.
complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
followUp: How would rendezvous hashing reduce movement when a shard is added?
situation: Shard placement must be stable across processes. A randomized hash sends the same key to different shards after restart.
guarantee: Map each integer key to a shard index in [0, shard_count) with a deterministic modulo.
edges: Modulo yields the shard index.
Do not use process-randomized hashes for an integer id.
shard_count is positive.
failureGuide: Use a stable key % shard_count (or language equivalent for the typed integer).

title: Rollout batches
prompt: Split an ordered host list into rollout waves without exceeding the specified batch size.
constraints: batch_size is a positive integer. Preserve order and duplicates. Every batch except the last must contain batch_size hosts. Empty input returns an empty list.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: A rollout batch is a contiguous slice of the host list, not a random sample.
Move a window of width batch_size across the list until you pass the end.
for i in range(0, len(hosts), batch_size): yield hosts[i:i+batch_size].
explanation: Batching bounds simultaneous changes, but healthy gates between waves are still required before this becomes a safe deployment workflow.
complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
followUp: What evidence would make you pause before starting the next batch?
solution:
def rollout_batches(hosts, batch_size):
    return [hosts[index:index + batch_size] for index in range(0, len(hosts), batch_size)]
situation: Canary batches limit blast radius. Off-by-one slices either skip hosts or dump the remainder into one unsafe batch.
guarantee: Split hosts into contiguous batches of batch_size, with a final shorter batch if needed.
edges: Advance the start index by batch_size each time.
A slice handles the final partial batch.
Empty hosts yield no batches.
failureGuide: Check step size and that the last batch may be shorter than batch_size.

title: Hosts low on disk
prompt: Evaluate normalized disk usage without dividing by an unknown capacity.
constraints: Each disk has name, used and capacity (nonnegative integers). threshold_percent is 0–100. Include disks with positive capacity and used/capacity*100 >= threshold. Preserve input order. Zero capacity is unknown and excluded.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Pressure is used versus capacity at a percent threshold, not a free-space vibe check.
Skip or refuse zero capacity per the criteria. Compare used * 100 against capacity * threshold without dividing first.
if capacity > 0 and used * 100 >= capacity * threshold_percent: include the disk.
explanation: An exact integer comparison treats the boundary correctly. Unknown capacity requires a separate telemetry check rather than a fabricated utilization.
complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
followUp: Which other signals would distinguish nearly full storage from an imminent outage?
solution:
def pressured_disks(disks, threshold_percent):
    return [disk["name"] for disk in disks if disk["capacity"] > 0 and disk["used"] * 100 >= threshold_percent * disk["capacity"]]
situation: Disk pressure alerts prevent full volumes. Division rounding can hide a disk that is already over the threshold.
guarantee: Return disks whose used/capacity ratio meets the threshold, using a comparison that avoids float rounding traps.
edges: Guard capacity before comparing utilization.
Cross multiplication avoids division error.
Do not mutate the input.
failureGuide: Check zero capacity handling and whether you used cross multiplication against the threshold.

title: Secrets in a structured log
prompt: Remove sensitive values from nested JSON logs before exporting them to an observability backend.
constraints: Recursively handle dictionaries, lists and JSON scalars. Replace values of case-insensitive keys password, token and authorization with "[REDACTED]". Preserve key spelling and all other values. Input keys are strings.
Do not mutate input values. Use the Python standard library only.
hints: Redaction is a structural walk: containers are rebuilt, scalars pass through, sensitive keys swap their values.
Branch on type. For mappings, decide per key whether to replace the value or recurse. For sequences, map redact over items.
if dict: {k: ("[REDACTED]" if k.lower() in sensitive else redact(v)) for k,v in ...}; if list: [redact(x) for x in ...]; else return value.
explanation: Build new containers recursively. This policy is intentionally explicit; it does not detect secrets embedded in arbitrary free text.
complexity: O(n) time and space for all visited values; O(depth) recursion stack.
followUp: How would you test this policy against newly introduced credential fields without logging the credentials?
situation: Logs leaving the box can carry passwords. Missing a nested key leaks a secret; over-redacting hides useful fields.
guarantee: Recursively copy structures, replacing values under case-insensitive keys password, token, and authorization with "[REDACTED]".
edges: Handle dicts, lists, and scalars separately.
Redact on the key before recursing into that value.
Preserve key spelling for non-sensitive fields.
failureGuide: Recurse into nested maps and lists. Compare keys case-insensitively only for the three sensitive names.
